title: How STR Regulation Actually Works: Licensing, Zoning & Primary-Residence Rules
section: Part One · Module 3 - STR Regulations & Compliance

slides.title: Permission attaches to one address, one use, and one person
slides.subtitle: Lesson 3.1. How STR Regulation Actually Works: Licensing, Zoning & Primary-Residence Rules
meta: Education only. Not legal advice. Rules change, so check official pages.
slides.notes:
Before any numbers matter, you need permission to run a short-term rental at one exact address. It's the check most students skip, and it's the one that can end a deal outright.

Two terms first. A short-term rental, or STR, is a furnished stay of less than about a month, the kind booked on Airbnb or Vrbo. Rental arbitrage means you lease a unit from a landlord, you don't live in it, and you rent it to short-stay guests. Most of this lesson asks whether that model is allowed at one address.

By the end you'll be able to list every layer of permission for that address, from the state down to your lease. You'll know which answers have to come in writing, and from whom. What you walk away with is a permission ladder with a result: permitted, prohibited, or unresolved.

We'll use a hypothetical unit called Alder Street, and we'll drop it into two real rulebooks, New York City and Los Angeles. Rules change often, so treat this as education, not legal advice, and check the official pages on the day you research.

slides.eyebrow: The wrong question: "Is Airbnb legal in this city?"
slides.text: Think of permission as a ladder. Every rung can say no, and you need a yes on every rung for your exact use.
slides.support: A city may allow short stays in general while the building, the zoning, the permit category, or your lease blocks the unit you want.
slides.notes:
Students often ask me whether a city is Airbnb-friendly. That label doesn't help you. Permission attaches to an address, a use, and a person.

Picture a ladder. Each rung is a separate question that can end the deal. Some rungs come from an authority: the state, the zoning, the permit program, the building, the HOA, your lease. Others come from the details of the permit rules. You need a yes on every rung, for your exact use. One no anywhere ends the deal, even when every other rung says yes.

Airbnb's own regulations overview says many cities require you to register, get a permit, or get a license before you list or take guests. It also flags zoning and taxes. That page is a fine starting point. It isn't the final word for any address. The final word is the official ordinance, the city office that runs it, and the documents that bind your building and your lease.

slides.title: Six layers can each say no, and each has its own source document
rows: Statewide rules, tax registration, limits on cities
Whether short stays are allowed in this district, or only as a side use of someone's home (accessory use)
Category, eligibility, fees, caps, renewal, number to display
The licensing program's page and ordinance
Occupancy limits, alarms, exits, excluded building types
Private bans filed in the property records
Whether the owner allows the use, in writing, and signs any permit consent
Lease clause or signed addendum; any city consent form
slides.caption: Also check: your insurer covers guests here, and the platform accepts your number (lesson 3.3).
slides.notes:
Work from the widest authority down to the narrowest. Each layer has its own document. Later, the ladder breaks these six layers into 15 specific questions.

The state may set rules that apply everywhere, like lodging tax registration or limits on what cities can regulate. Many states leave most of this to local governments, but check before you assume.

Zoning decides what uses a parcel may have. Some residential zones treat short stays as commercial lodging and ban them. Others allow them only as an accessory use, meaning a side use of someone's home.

Many cities then run a separate permit program on top of zoning. That's where the category, eligibility, caps, fees, and your display number live.

Building and fire codes can set occupancy limits and alarm rules, and some programs exclude certain building types.

A homeowners association, condo, or co-op can have rules filed in the property records that ban short rentals, even where the city allows them.

And for arbitrage, the lease is the layer you control least. Some cities also want the landlord's signed consent on the permit application. Lessons 3.5 and 5.3 cover those documents.

slides.title: Arbitrage is unhosted, so the host-present clause often settles the question

left.head: Hosted stay
items: The host lives in the unit
The host is present during the stay
Guests usually rent a room
Looks like a resident earning from a spare room

right.head: Unhosted stay
items: Guests have the whole unit
Nobody lives there
This is the arbitrage model: you lease it and live elsewhere
Looks like a hotel room taken from housing supply

box.label: Read this first
box.text: When you open an ordinance, find the words that decide whether the host must be present. That one clause often settles the question before anything else.

slides.notes:
A hosted stay means the host lives in the unit and is there during the stay. Usually the guest rents a room while the host is home. An unhosted stay means guests have the whole place and nobody lives there.

Cities treat these two very differently. A hosted stay looks like a resident earning some income from a spare room. An unhosted stay looks like a hotel room carved out of the housing supply. So many cities allow the first and restrict or ban the second.

Arbitrage is almost always unhosted. You lease a whole unit and you live somewhere else.

So here's a habit I want you to build. When you open an ordinance, don't start at the top and read every word. Search for the clause that decides whether the host must be present. That one clause often answers the question for an arbitrage plan before you read anything else.

slides.title: A primary-residence rule is usually a hard stop for arbitrage
items: You may host only in the home where you actually live
Cities usually define it by time, such as more than half the year (Los Angeles: more than six months)
Some also require it to be the only property where you host
Cities may ask for proof: driver's license, voter registration, or tax records at that address
Signing a lease on a unit while you live elsewhere doesn't make it your primary residence
slides.notes:
A primary-residence rule says you may only host in the home where you actually live. Cities usually define that by time, like living there more than half the year. Some add that it has to be the only property where you host.

For an arbitrage operator, this is usually a hard stop. You can't turn a unit into your primary residence just by signing a lease on it while you live across town. And cities that use this rule often check. They may ask for a driver's license, voter registration, or tax records showing that address.

So when you read a city's rules, look for this test right after the hosted or unhosted clause. If the city has a primary-residence rule and you don't live in the unit, the arbitrage plan fails at this rung. You don't need to go further down the ladder.

slides.title: Night caps hit arbitrage hardest because rent is due all 12 months
columns: Why it matters for a lease
rows: Nights per year you may host. Some cities cap only unhosted nights.
The math has to work on the capped nights alone
How many permits the city issues, sometimes by neighborhood or district
New applicants may land on a waitlist
How many permits one person or one building may hold
Limits scaling in one building or one name

box.label: This fails if
box.text: The city lets you host only part of the year. Your rent is still due every month. Later in this lesson, a 120-night cap turns our example unit into a $10,445 annual loss.

slides.notes:
Caps come in three forms.

A night cap limits how many nights a year you may host. Some cities cap only unhosted nights and leave hosted nights alone.

A permit cap limits how many permits the city hands out, sometimes by neighborhood or zoning district. If the cap is full, new applicants may go on a waitlist.

A unit cap limits how many permits one person or one building can hold.

Of the three, the night cap hurts arbitrage the most. Your rent is due twelve months a year. If the city lets you host only part of the year, the math has to work on those nights alone. The rest of the year is pure cost. In the worked example you'll see how fast that fails. At a 120-night cap, our example unit loses $10,445 a year.

slides.title: Many cities draw the short-term line at 30 nights, so count the way they do
items: Many cities define a short-term rental by stay length, often under 30 nights
Stays at or above the line often count as ordinary residential tenancies
Count the way your city counts: New York City's FAQ says 29 nights is short-term and 30 is not
Read your city's own definition before you set a minimum stay

box.label: Longer stays are not a loophole
box.text: Past the threshold, tenant protections can apply, including eviction procedures and rent rules, depending on the state and city. Treat month-plus furnished rentals as a separate business and have an attorney review it.

slides.notes:
Many cities define a short-term rental by how long the guest stays, often under 30 nights. At or above that line, the stay is often treated as an ordinary residential tenancy, depending on the state and city. Those follow different rules.

Check how your city counts the length of a stay. New York City's FAQ spells out its rule. It treats the check-in date as day zero, under state law. By its count, a 29-night stay is short-term and a 30-night stay is not. Your city may count differently, so read its own definition.

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. Just take 30-night bookings and skip the rules. That isn't a loophole. Once a guest stays past the threshold, tenant protections can apply. That can mean eviction procedures and rent rules if a guest won't leave.

So treat month-plus furnished rentals as a separate business, with its own rules. Have an attorney review it before you try it.

slides.title: Never assume a permit transfers: ask who holds it, and get the answer in writing
slides.text: Some cities issue the permit to the property owner, some to the host, and some tie it to both. Three situations expose the difference:
items: You take over a unit that "already has a permit." If it belongs to the previous host, it may not cover you.
The landlord sells the building. A permit issued to the owner may end with the sale.
You add a partner or form an LLC. Some programs require a natural person (an individual, not a company), so an entity may not qualify.
slides.notes:
Here's a question students rarely ask: who does the permit belong to? Some cities issue it to the property owner. Some issue it to the host, meaning the person who lives there or runs the rental. Some tie it to both.

That matters in three situations.

First, a landlord tells you the unit already has a permit. If that permit belongs to the previous host, it may not cover you at all.

Second, the landlord sells the building. If the permit was issued to the owner, it may end with the sale, and you're left with a lease and no permission.

Third, you bring in a partner or set up an LLC. Some programs require the host to be a natural person, meaning an individual, not a company. An LLC may not qualify.

So never assume a permit transfers. Ask the licensing office in writing, and keep the reply in your deal folder.

slides.eyebrow: New York City · Local Law 18 registration
slides.title: New York City: the host must live there, stay home, and host two guests at most
items: Hosts must register with the city, or the rental is illegal
The host must be a natural person who lives there, and certify the lease allows short-term rentals
The host stays in the unit with guests. No more than two paying guests at a time.
No entire apartment or home for less than 30 days, in any permanent residential building
Platforms must verify the registration number, legal name, and address before collecting a fee
Owners can put a building on the Prohibited Buildings List; the city's enforcement office (OSE) must then deny registration
slides.notes:
Let's look at two big cities with very different rules. I'm using them to show how much the answer changes with the address. Rules change, so check the official pages on the day you research.

New York City's program is Local Law 18, run by the Office of Special Enforcement, or OSE. Hosts must register, or the rental is illegal. The host has to be a natural person who lives there, and must certify that the lease doesn't prohibit short-term rentals.

The host has to stay in the unit with the guests. No more than two paying guests. Guests share the home with the host, and they must be able to use the whole unit. You cannot rent an entire apartment for less than 30 days.

The registration number goes in every ad. Booking platforms can't collect a fee unless they've checked the city's verification system. And building owners can list a building on the Prohibited Buildings List, which means OSE must deny registration there.

Also on the city's pages: the fee is $145, non-refundable. Airbnb says hosts awaiting approval can set a 30-night minimum. That's a holding pattern while you wait. It doesn't get you around the rules.

slides.title: Los Angeles: primary residence only, with a 120-day yearly cap unless Extended
items: Primary residence only: more than six months a year, and your only home-share
Up to 120 days a year; Extended Home-Sharing adds criteria, like six months registered
Rent-stabilized (RSO) units excluded: most multifamily built before Oct 1, 1978; check the city's ZIMAS parcel tool, Housing tab
Renters submit the landlord's written, notarized approval
Register for the city's hotel tax (Transient Occupancy Tax, TOT) and show the number on every listing
slides.notes:
Los Angeles runs a Home-Sharing Ordinance. City Planning handles registration and the housing department explains who's eligible.

Home-sharing is limited to your primary residence, where you live more than six months of the year. It must also be the only property where you home-share. The standard limit is 120 days per calendar year. Going beyond that takes an Extended Home-Sharing registration, with extra criteria, including holding a regular registration for at least six months.

Units under the Rent Stabilization Ordinance aren't eligible. That's most multifamily units built before October 1, 1978. You can check RSO status by address in the city's ZIMAS parcel tool, under the Housing tab.

A renter has to submit the landlord's written, notarized approval. Hosts register for the city's hotel tax, the Transient Occupancy Tax, and post the number on every listing.

Also on the city's pages: the FAQ lists an $89 fee, with extended review at $850, or $5,660 when a case-by-case review is required. Confirm current fees with City Planning, since FAQ documents can lag.

So both cities allow some short-term renting. Neither allows the arbitrage model we'll test next.

slides.title: Alder Street: one hypothetical unit, dropped into two real rulebooks
items: Unit 4B, 218 Alder Street: two bedrooms, sleeps 5, in a four-unit building
The student leases it and lives somewhere else
Plan: unhosted, whole-unit stays averaging 3 nights
70% occupancy = 255 nights a year
All figures are teaching assumptions; the real city is unnamed on purpose
slides.notes:
Now the worked example. Alder Street is the course's running example, the same unit other lessons use. It's Unit 4B at 218 Alder Street, a hypothetical two-bedroom that sleeps five, in a four-unit building.

The student leases it from the landlord and lives somewhere else. That's the arbitrage model. The plan is unhosted, whole-unit stays averaging three nights, at 70% occupancy. That works out to 255 nights a year.

Every number here is an assumption for teaching. The real city is left unnamed on purpose, because rules attach to an exact address. So instead we'll drop the same unit into two real rulebooks, New York City and Los Angeles, and watch how the answer changes.

slides.eyebrow: Worked example · Alder Street in New York City
slides.title: In New York City, Alder Street fails five of six rules, and any one of them ends it
rows: Host is a natural person and permanent occupant
Host present in the unit during the stay
No more than two paying guests
No entire unit for less than 30 days
Building not on the Prohibited Buildings List
Registration number on every ad; platform verifies it
slides.caption: Result: **prohibited** as planned. The entire-unit rule alone ends it. Switching to 30-night stays or a hosted room makes it a different business.
slides.notes:
First, New York City. The host has to be the permanent occupant, the person who lives there. Alder Street's operator lives elsewhere. Fails. The host has to be present. It's unhosted. Fails. Two paying guests at most, and it sleeps five. Fails. No entire unit under 30 days, and the plan is three-night stays. Fails.

Without meeting those, the operator can't register, so there's no number for the platform to verify. Fails. The Prohibited Buildings List is the only row we'd still have to check, and at this point it doesn't matter.

Result: prohibited. The entire-unit rule alone ends it. Switching to 30-night stays makes it a different business under tenant law, which we covered earlier. And a hosted room with the host present isn't arbitrage anymore. Either way, the plan we started with doesn't survive New York.
slides.keyline: Alder Street is hypothetical (its figures are assumptions); the rules come from each city's official pages.

slides.eyebrow: Worked example · Alder Street in Los Angeles
slides.title: In Los Angeles, the primary-residence rule alone ends Alder Street
rows: Primary residence (more than 6 months a year)
Only property where the host home-shares
Four-unit building; depends on build date and other facts
Up to 120 days a year unless Extended
Lease offered; approval not yet signed
TOT registration and number on every listing
slides.caption: Result: **prohibited** as planned. In LA: primary residence and the night cap. In NYC (previous slide): the host-present and whole-unit rules.
slides.notes:
Now drop the same unit into Los Angeles.

Primary residence, meaning the host lives there more than six months a year. The operator lives elsewhere, so it fails. It must be the only property where the host home-shares. This would be a second property, so it fails. RSO status depends on when the building was built and other facts, so that's a ZIMAS check. The plan is 255 nights, and the standard cap is 120 days, so it fails. The notarized landlord approval and the tax registration are still open.

Result: prohibited. The primary-residence rule ends it on its own, and the night cap would end it too.

Notice what happened across these two slides. The same unit, the same lease, and the same math got two different no answers for two different reasons. That's why "is this city Airbnb-friendly" doesn't help you.
slides.keyline: Alder Street is hypothetical (its figures are assumptions); the rules come from each city's official pages.

slides.title: As a business, 120 nights can't carry Alder Street's $23,400 rent: -$10,445 a year
slides.side: About -$870 a month. Every other assumption stays the same. Compare: +$12,218 a year at the planned 255 nights.

side_box.label: To break even
side_box.text: The nightly rate would need to reach about $308, roughly 50% above the $205 base rate. If the student really lived there, part of the rent would be their own housing: a different plan.

slides.notes:
Suppose someone tried to fix the Los Angeles problem. Move in, make it your primary residence, and host within the 120-day cap. I'll treat that as 120 booked nights and run it as a business test, keeping every other assumption the same.

One hundred twenty nights at $205 is $24,600. At three nights a stay, that's 40 stays, and $110 cleaning each adds $4,400. That's $29,000 of gross bookings. Airbnb's host-only fee, 15.5% of nightly plus cleaning, takes $4,495. Cleaner and supplies for 40 stays take $4,360. Then the fixed costs arrive in full: $23,400 of rent, plus utilities, insurance, software, repairs, and the permit, for $30,590.

Net is minus $10,445 a year, about minus $870 a month. At the planned 255 nights it was plus $12,218.

To break even, the nightly rate would need to reach about $308, roughly 50% above the base rate. This counts the full rent as a business cost. If the student really lives there, part of that rent is their own housing, and that's home-sharing, a different plan. As an arbitrage business, a 120-night cap doesn't work at this rent.

slides.title: Work every address down the same chain, and stop at the first no

nodes.d: Address, parcel, hosted or not, guests, stay length, nights. Confirm the real jurisdiction.
The official code and program page. Stop if it bans your model.
Zoning, building type, listed buildings, HOA, lease.
Category, eligibility, caps, fees, renewal, transfer, number display.
Written question to the office. Save dated evidence. Record a result and recheck date.

box.label: Official sources only
box.text: A blog post, a Facebook group, or another host's opinion is not a source. Sam's 3.2 runs this flow live on a real address.

slides.notes:
Here's the flow I want you to follow for every address. Nine steps, grouped into five boxes.

Write down the exact plan first: address, unit, parcel number, hosted or unhosted, maximum guests, stay length, nights per year. Then confirm which jurisdictions apply. Many students check the wrong city because of a mailing address. Use the city or county parcel lookup to get the parcel number, the ID the county gives each lot.

Find the official ordinance and the program's own page. Airbnb's city pages can point you there. A blog or a Facebook group is not a source. If the ordinance bans your model, stop.

Check the parcel and building: zoning, building type, rent-regulation status, any list like New York's. Then private rules: HOA and the lease. Then permit mechanics. Each has a stop exit.

If anything is unclear, ask the licensing office a specific yes-or-no question in writing. Save a dated PDF of every page and reply. Put them in the deal folder with SR.1, the regulatory compliance checklist in the course resources. Record permitted, prohibited, or unresolved. Unresolved means you don't sign yet.

slides.title: One No on any rung means prohibited, and one Unclear means unresolved
rows: Do state rules allow this plan here (or leave it to the city)?
Does this zoning district allow the planned use?
Is there a permit category my plan fits?
Can I meet any primary-residence test (or is there none)?
Do my planned nights per year fit under any night cap?
Can I get a permit now, without a waitlist?
slides.caption: Rungs 1 to 7 of 15. Every question is written so Yes is good. Write the plan facts first: address, parcel, jurisdiction, hosted or not, guests, stay length, nights, named host.
slides.notes:
This is the exercise, the permission ladder. Fill it in for one real address. No address yet? Use a rental listing you'd realistically consider in your target city. If you want the full version, use SR.1, the regulatory compliance checklist in the course resources.

Before the ladder, write the plan facts. Full address and unit, parcel number, jurisdiction, hosted or unhosted, maximum guests, typical stay length, and nights per year. Add who will be the named host or permit holder. Every answer below depends on those facts.

Every question is written so that Yes is the good answer. For an arbitrage plan, do the hosted, primary-residence, and night-cap rungs first. Any one of them can end the plan quickly.

Every answer, yes or no, needs an official source link and the date you checked it. If the ordinance is unclear, write unclear and send the licensing office a question.

The rule is strict on purpose. One no on any rung means prohibited for this plan. One unclear means unresolved.

slides.title: The last eight rungs test the building, private rules, insurance, and the permit
rows: Is my typical stay allowed, counted the city's way?
Is the building eligible (not rent-regulated, affordable, or listed)?
Can I meet the required inspections and equipment?
Do recorded rules allow it, or is there none?
Does the lease allow it, with any required consent?
Will an insurer cover guests under my permit?
Will the permit be in my name and survive a sale?
Can I show the number and pass platform checks?
slides.caption: Decision: Permitted / Prohibited / Unresolved, with a recheck date and reviewer. No lease if unresolved.
slides.notes:
The last eight rungs are where the private documents and the permit's fine print come in. Same rule: Yes is always the good answer.

Minimum stay: is your typical stay allowed, counted the way the city counts? Building type: is the building eligible, meaning not rent-regulated, affordable, or on a prohibited list? Safety and inspection: can you meet what the city requires before it issues a permit?

Then the private layers. Do the HOA, condo, or co-op documents allow it? Does the lease or a signed addendum allow it, and can you get any landlord consent the city requires, the way Los Angeles does?

Insurance: will an insurer cover short-term guests at this address, under your permit category? Transferability: will the permit be in your name, and survive a sale or a change of operator? And number display: can you show the number where required and pass the platform's check?

At the bottom, write your decision, a recheck date, and who reviewed it. Don't sign a lease on an unresolved address.

slides.title: Six parties confirm permission, and each answer should be in writing
rows: Whether your exact plan fits a permit category at this address, and who the permit holder must be
That the parcel's zoning district allows the use
That the lease and addendum allow the use, and whether stays of 30+ nights create a tenancy
That recorded rules allow short-term rentals
A signed consent to use the address on a permit application, separate from the lease (LA: notarized affidavit)
That the policy covers short-term guests at this address under your permit category
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

The city or county licensing office confirms, in writing, whether your exact plan fits a permit category at this address. It also confirms who the permit holder has to be.

The zoning or planning department confirms the parcel's district allows the use.

An attorney licensed in your state confirms that the lease and any addendum allow the use. They also tell you whether stays of 30 nights or more would create a tenancy.

If there's an HOA, condo, or co-op board, get their answer in writing too.

The landlord signs a document that lets you use the address on a permit application. That's separate from the lease or addendum that allows short stays. Some cities require a specific form. Los Angeles, for example, uses a notarized affidavit.

And your insurer confirms the policy covers short-term guests at this address, under the permit category you'll actually hold. Save every one of these in the deal folder.

slides.title: Work one real address down the ladder this week, before you sign anything

Find the official ordinance and permit program page, and save dated PDFs of both.
Search the ordinance for the host-present, primary-residence, and night-cap clauses, and mark those rungs.
Send the licensing office one specific yes-or-no question about your plan, in writing.

slides.notes:
Four things to do this week, each under an hour.

Write the plan facts for one real address. Get the parcel number from the city or county parcel lookup, and confirm which jurisdiction it's actually in.

Find the official ordinance and the permit program's own page. Save dated PDFs of both.

Search the ordinance for three clauses: whether the host must be present, whether there's a primary-residence test, and whether there's a night cap. Mark those rungs on your ladder.

Then send the licensing office one specific yes-or-no question about your plan, in writing.

slides.notes:
These are the main sources behind the lesson. All were checked on September 25, 2026. The full list in the lesson has a few more. It adds the New York registration rules page, the Local Law 18 text, and Airbnb's New York page. It also adds the Los Angeles landlord affidavit and the earlier Los Angeles FAQ.

Notice the pattern. Airbnb's regulations overview is the starting point. The rules themselves come from the city: the Office of Special Enforcement in New York, and City Planning and the housing department in Los Angeles.

When you work your own address, your sources list should look like this. Official pages, each with the date you checked. If you can only find a blog post or a forum thread, write unresolved and send the licensing office a question.

The Alder Street figures, including the 120-night scenario and the $308 break-even rate, were computed from the canonical inputs. They're assumptions for teaching.
